source: Ere quitting, for the nonce, the Sperm Whale’s head, I would have you, as a sensible physiologist, simply—particularly remark its front aspect, in all its compacted collectedness. I would have you investigate it now with the sole view of forming to yourself some unexaggerated, intelligent estimate of whatever battering-ram power may be lodged there. Here is a vital point; for you must either satisfactorily settle this matter with yourself, or for ever remain an infidel as to one of the most appalling, but not the less true events, perhaps anywhere to be found in all recorded history.

You observe that in the ordinary swimming position of the Sperm Whale, the front of his head presents an almost wholly vertical plane to the water; you observe that the lower part of that front slopes considerably backwards, so as to furnish more of a retreat for the long socket which receives the boom-like lower jaw; you observe that the mouth is entirely under the head, much in the same way, indeed, as though your own mouth were entirely under your chin. Moreover you observe that the whale has no external nose; and that what nose he has—his spout hole—is on the top of his head; you observe that his eyes and ears are at the sides of his head, nearly one third of his entire length from the front. Wherefore, you must now have perceived that the front of the Sperm Whale’s head is a dead, blind wall, without a single organ or tender prominence of any sort whatsoever. Furthermore, you are now to consider that only in the extreme, lower, backward sloping part of the front of the head, is there the slightest vestige of bone; and not till you get near twenty feet from the forehead do you come to the full cranial development. So that this whole enormous boneless mass is as one wad. Finally, though, as will soon be revealed, its contents partly comprise the most delicate oil; yet, you are now to be apprised of the nature of the substance which so impregnably invests all that apparent effeminacy. In some previous place I have described to you how the blubber wraps the body of the whale, as the rind wraps an orange. Just so with the head; but with this difference: about the head this envelope, though not so thick, is of a boneless toughness, inestimable by any man who has not handled it. The severest pointed harpoon, the sharpest lance darted by the strongest human arm, impotently rebounds from it. It is as though the forehead of the Sperm Whale were paved with horses’ hoofs. I do not think that any sensation lurks in it.

Bethink yourself also of another thing. When two large, loaded Indiamen chance to crowd and crush towards each other in the docks, what do the sailors do? They do not suspend between them, at the point of coming contact, any merely hard substance, like iron or wood. No, they hold there a large, round wad of tow and cork, enveloped in the thickest and toughest of ox-hide. That bravely and uninjured takes the jam which would have snapped all their oaken handspikes and iron crow-bars. By itself this sufficiently illustrates the obvious fact I drive at. But supplementary to this, it has hypothetically occurred to me, that as ordinary fish possess what is called a swimming bladder in them, capable, at will, of distension or contraction; and as the Sperm Whale, as far as I know, has no such provision in him; considering, too, the otherwise inexplicable manner in which he now depresses his head altogether beneath the surface, and anon swims with it high elevated out of the water; considering the unobstructed elasticity of its envelope; considering the unique interior of his head; it has hypothetically occurred to me, I say, that those mystical lung-celled honeycombs there may possibly have some hitherto unknown and unsuspected connexion with the outer air, so as to be susceptible to atmospheric distension and contraction. If this be so, fancy the irresistibleness of that might, to which the most impalpable and destructive of all elements contributes.

Now, mark. Unerringly impelling this dead, impregnable, uninjurable wall, and this most buoyant thing within; there swims behind it all a mass of tremendous life, only to be adequately estimated as piled wood is—by the cord; and all obedient to one volition, as the smallest insect. So that when I shall hereafter detail to you all the specialities and concentrations of potency everywhere lurking in this expansive monster; when I shall show you some of his more inconsiderable braining feats; I trust you will have renounced all ignorant incredulity, and be ready to abide by this; that though the Sperm Whale stove a passage through the Isthmus of Darien, and mixed the Atlantic with the Pacific, you would not elevate one hair of your eye-brow. For unless you own the whale, you are but a provincial and sentimentalist in Truth. But clear Truth is a thing for salamander giants only to encounter; how small the chances for the provincials then? What befell the weakling youth lifting the dread goddess’s veil at Lais?

modern_en.title: Chapter 76 — The Battering-Ram
paragraphs: Before leaving the Sperm Whale's head for now, I would have you, as a sensible physiologist, simply — and particularly — take note of its front, in all its compact concentration. I would have you examine it now with the single aim of forming for yourself some unexaggerated, intelligent estimate of whatever battering-ram power may be lodged there. This is a vital point, for you must either settle this matter to your own satisfaction, or remain forever an unbeliever about one of the most appalling, but no less true, events to be found perhaps anywhere in all recorded history.

You observe that in the ordinary swimming position of the Sperm Whale, the front of his head presents an almost entirely vertical surface to the water. You observe that the lower part of that front slopes considerably backward, so as to leave more room for the long socket that receives the boom-like lower jaw. You observe that the mouth is entirely under the head, much as though your own mouth were entirely under your chin. Moreover, you observe that the whale has no external nose, and that what nose he has — his spout hole — is on the top of his head; you observe that his eyes and ears are at the sides of his head, nearly one third of his entire length back from the front. So you must by now have realized that the front of the Sperm Whale's head is a dead, blind wall, without a single organ or tender projection of any kind whatsoever. Furthermore, you must now consider that only in the extreme, lower, backward-sloping part of the front of the head is there the slightest trace of bone, and that not until you get nearly twenty feet back from the forehead do you come to the full development of the skull. So this whole enormous boneless mass is like one wad. Finally, although, as will soon be revealed, its contents partly consist of the most delicate oil, you must now be told the nature of the substance that so impregnably encases all that apparent delicacy. Earlier I described to you how the blubber wraps the body of the whale as the rind wraps an orange. It is just the same with the head, but with this difference: around the head this envelope, though not so thick, has a boneless toughness that no one who has not handled it can imagine. The most sharply pointed harpoon, the keenest lance thrown by the strongest human arm, bounces off it powerlessly. It is as though the forehead of the Sperm Whale were paved with horses' hoofs. I do not think that any sensation lurks in it.

Think of another thing, too. When two large, loaded Indiamen — big merchant ships of the India trade — happen to crowd and crush toward each other in the docks, what do the sailors do? They do not hang between them, at the point where they will touch, any merely hard substance, like iron or wood. No, they hold there a large, round wad of tow (coarse flax or hemp fiber) and cork, wrapped in the thickest and toughest of ox-hide. That wad bravely and without injury takes the squeeze that would have snapped all their oak handspikes and iron crowbars. By itself this is enough to illustrate the obvious fact I am driving at. But in addition to this, it has occurred to me as a hypothesis that, since ordinary fish have what is called a swimming bladder, which they can swell or shrink at will; and since the Sperm Whale, as far as I know, has no such equipment; considering, too, the otherwise unaccountable way in which he sometimes sinks his head completely beneath the surface, and at other times swims with it raised high out of the water; considering the unobstructed elasticity of its envelope; considering the unique interior of his head — it has occurred to me as a hypothesis, I say, that those mystical, lung-celled honeycombs in there may possibly have some hitherto unknown and unsuspected connection with the outer air, so that they can be swelled and shrunk by the atmosphere. If this is so, imagine the irresistible force of that might, when the most impalpable and destructive of all the elements contributes to it.

Now, notice this. Driving this dead, impregnable, uninjurable wall unerringly forward, and this most buoyant thing inside it, there swims behind it all a mass of tremendous life, which can only be properly measured the way piled wood is — by the cord; and all of it obeys a single will, as the smallest insect does. So when I later describe to you in detail all the special powers and concentrations of force lurking everywhere in this vast monster, and show you some of his lesser feats of head-smashing, I trust you will have given up all ignorant disbelief and be ready to stand by this: that even if the Sperm Whale smashed a passage through the Isthmus of Darien, in Panama, and mixed the Atlantic with the Pacific, you would not raise one hair of your eyebrow. For unless you acknowledge the whale, you are only a provincial and a sentimentalist in Truth. But clear Truth is something only salamander giants can face; how small, then, are the chances for the provincials? What happened to the feeble youth who lifted the veil of the dread goddess at Lais?

modern_da.title: Kapitel 76 — Murbrækkeren
paragraphs: Før jeg for nu forlader kaskelottens hoved, vil jeg gerne, at du som fornuftig fysiolog helt enkelt — og særligt — lægger mærke til dets forside i hele dens samlede koncentration. Jeg vil gerne, at du nu undersøger den med det ene formål at danne dig et uoverdrevet, fornuftigt skøn over, hvilken rambukkraft der kan ligge der. Dette er et afgørende punkt, for du må enten afgøre sagen til din egen tilfredshed eller for evigt forblive vantro over for en af de mest rædselsfulde, men ikke mindre sande hændelser, der måske findes noget sted i hele den nedskrevne historie.

Du ser, at i kaskelottens almindelige svømmestilling vender forsiden af hovedet en næsten helt lodret flade mod vandet. Du ser, at den nederste del af forsiden skråner kraftigt bagud, så der bliver mere plads til den lange hulning, der modtager den bomagtige underkæbe. Du ser, at munden ligger helt under hovedet, omtrent som om din egen mund lå helt under hagen. Desuden ser du, at hvalen ikke har nogen ydre næse, og at den næse, han har — blæsehullet — sidder oven på hans hoved. Du ser, at hans øjne og ører sidder på siderne af hovedet, næsten en tredjedel af hele hans længde bag fra forenden. Så du må nu have indset, at forsiden af kaskelottens hoved er en død, blind mur uden et eneste organ eller ømt fremspring af nogen art overhovedet. Videre må du nu overveje, at kun yderst nede, i den bagudskrånende del af hovedets forside, findes det mindste spor af knogle, og at du først når næsten tyve fod tilbage fra panden kommer til skallens fulde udvikling. Så hele denne enorme knogleløse masse er som én stor prop. Endelig, selv om dens indhold, som snart skal vises, delvis består af den fineste olie, må du nu høre om arten af det stof, der så ubetvingeligt omslutter al denne tilsyneladende ømhed. Tidligere har jeg beskrevet for dig, hvordan spækket omslutter hvalens krop, som skallen omslutter en appelsin. Det er nøjagtig det samme med hovedet, men med den forskel, at omkring hovedet har denne indpakning, skønt ikke så tyk, en knogleløs sejhed, som ingen, der ikke har rørt ved den, kan forestille sig. Den skarpest spidsede harpun, den hvasseste lanse, kastet af den stærkeste menneskearm, preller magtesløst af på den. Det er, som om kaskelottens pande var brolagt med hestehove. Jeg tror ikke, at der gemmer sig nogen følelse i den.

Tænk også på noget andet. Når to store, tungt lastede Indiafarere — store handelsskibe på Indienfart — støder sammen og presses mod hinanden inde i dokkerne, hvad gør sømændene så? De hænger ikke noget, der blot er hårdt, som jern eller træ, ned mellem dem på det sted, hvor de vil røre hinanden. Nej, de holder en stor, rund pude af værk (grove hør- eller hampefibre) og kork derned, svøbt i den tykkeste og sejeste oksehud. Den pude tager modigt og uden skade imod det tryk, der ville have knækket alle deres håndspager af eg og alle deres brækjern af jern. Alene det er nok til at belyse det åbenlyse, jeg er ude på. Men dertil kommer, at jeg har fået den tanke som en hypotese: Almindelige fisk har det, man kalder en svømmeblære, som de efter behag kan puste op eller trække sammen. Kaskelotten har, så vidt jeg ved, ikke noget sådant redskab. Dertil kommer den ellers uforklarlige måde, han nogle gange sænker hovedet helt ned under overfladen, og andre gange svømmer med det højt hævet over vandet. Dertil kommer den frie elasticitet i hovedets hylster, og dertil kommer hovedets enestående indre — og så har jeg altså fået den tanke som en hypotese, siger jeg, at de mystiske bikager af lungeceller derinde måske på en eller anden hidtil ukendt og uanet måde hænger sammen med den ydre luft, så de kan svulme op og skrumpe ind ved hjælp af atmosfæren. Hvis det er sådan, så forestil dig den uimodståelige kraft i den vælde, når det mest uhåndgribelige og ødelæggende af alle grundstoffer yder sit bidrag.

Læg nu mærke til dette. Denne døde, uigennemtrængelige, ubeskadigelige mur og det mest letbårne inde i den drives ufejlbarligt fremad af en kæmpemasse af liv, der svømmer bagved det hele, og som kun kan måles ordentligt på samme måde som stablet brænde — i favne — og som i sin helhed adlyder én eneste vilje, ligesom det mindste insekt gør. Når jeg derfor senere beskriver for dig i enkeltheder alle de særlige kræfter og kraftsamlinger, der lurer overalt i dette vældige uhyre, og viser dig nogle af hans mindre bedrifter i at knuse med hovedet, så regner jeg med, at du har lagt al uvidende vantro på hylden og er klar til at stå ved dette: at selv om kaskelotten brød sig vej gennem Darien-næsset i Panama og blandede Atlanterhavet med Stillehavet, ville du ikke løfte så meget som ét øjenbrynshår. For medmindre du anerkender hvalen, er du kun en provinsiel og en sentimentalist i Sandhed. Men den klare Sandhed kan kun salamanderkæmper se i øjnene; hvor små er så ikke chancerne for de provinsielle? Hvad skete der med den svage yngling, der løftede sløret for den frygtelige gudinde i Lais?
